project.name: qmix
project.description: QMix is a collaborative music player: a host runs playback on Google TV while friends add links from VK, Yandex Music, and Spotify to a shared queue, and a Go backend resolves those links to tracks and streams the audio. The project also includes a Kotlin/Jetpack Compose Android TV client and a guest PWA for adding tracks from a phone. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

nodes.name: vkyandex.go
nodes.summary: Resolves VK and Yandex Music links. Anonymously it scrapes og:title from the public page. With Config.VKToken set it resolves VK /audio{owner}_{id} links via the authenticated audio.getById VK API (v5.131, qmix#9); with Config.YMToken set it resolves Yandex Music /track/{id} links via an authenticated goym client against api.music.yandex.net (qmix#10). This is a major rewrite of the previous ~110-line anonymous-only Open Graph resolver.
nodes.languageNotes: Lazily constructs the goym client from vantuz's HTTP wrapper (rather than goym.New) to avoid an eager /account/status handshake; a sync.Mutex guards the cached client for concurrent resolves.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: QMix is a collaborative music player: a host runs playback on Google TV while friends paste VK, Yandex Music, or Spotify links into a shared queue from either the TV app or a browser-based guest PWA, and a Go backend resolves those links into playable tracks and streams the audio. The README tracks the project milestone by milestone -- room/queue management, link resolution, yt-dlp-backed streaming, authenticated resolvers for all three services, and the still-in-progress Android TV client -- and gives the fastest orientation to what exists today versus what's next.

tour.title: Go Backend Entry Point
tour.description: cmd/qmix/main.go is the process entry point for the qmix server binary. It delegates all --version and build-metadata handling to the shared buildinfo package (covered in a later step) so every QMix binary reports identical version information, then starts the HTTP server on the address given by QMIX_ADDR, defaulting to :8080.
tour.languageLesson: Go CLIs conventionally centralize flag/version handling in a shared helper (here buildinfo.Run) rather than duplicating it per binary -- keeping every entry point's --version output byte-for-byte consistent.

tour.title: Room Domain Model & Composition Root
tour.description: app.go is the composition root: it wires the in-memory room Store, the SSE Hub, the resolver Mux, and the stream backend into a single App and exposes it as an http.Handler. models.go defines the core domain types -- Room, Track, and Current -- while store.go implements a mutex-guarded store with collision-checked room-code generation and a TTL janitor that sweeps idle empty rooms, and code.go supplies the pluggable CodeGenerator behind that code generation.
tour.languageLesson: The CodeGenerator interface in code.go is a small dependency-injection seam: production code uses a random generator, while tests substitute a deterministic one -- a common Go pattern for keeping randomness testable.

tour.title: REST API & Real-Time Events
tour.description: handlers.go implements the Server's HTTP surface built on top of the Store from Step 3: room creation/lookup, host and guest track submission, skip/reorder queue mutations, and byte-range audio streaming. hub.go complements it with the per-room SSE fan-out hub, which streams an initial queue snapshot followed by live events and heartbeats to every connected client, using non-blocking publishes that disconnect slow subscribers rather than blocking the whole room.
tour.languageLesson: The hub's non-blocking channel send with an overflow-disconnect fallback is a standard Go pattern for fan-out broadcast: a slow reader must never be allowed to stall every other subscriber.

tour.title: The Guest PWA
tour.description: Not every friend has the TV remote, so QMix serves a lightweight, installable web app for adding tracks from a phone or laptop. guest_page.go embeds and serves the static assets -- index.html, app.js, and the web manifest -- gating the page behind a room-existence check. index.html renders a Material Design 3 queue view, app.js subscribes to the SSE stream from Step 4 with reconnect/backoff and submits new links via fetch, and manifest.webmanifest makes the page installable as a standalone app.
tour.languageLesson: Client-side reconnect/backoff on top of Server-Sent Events (rather than WebSockets) keeps the guest client simple: EventSource handles the long-lived connection, and app.js only needs to recover gracefully when it drops.

tour.title: Resolver Core Abstractions
tour.description: Before a link can join the queue, it has to become a Track. resolver.go defines that contract: the Track metadata struct, the Resolver interface, a set of sentinel errors (ErrInvalid, ErrUnsupported, ErrNoAnonymous, ErrService), and the Mux that dispatches an incoming URL to the right Resolver by domain. config.go and default.go wire this together for production, reading VK/Yandex/Spotify credentials from the environment via ConfigFromEnv and assembling the DefaultMux, while client.go supplies the shared 10-second bounded-timeout HTTP client every resolver falls back to.
tour.languageLesson: Sentinel errors (ErrNoAnonymous, ErrUnsupported, etc.) let callers use errors.Is to branch on failure kind without parsing error strings or defining a full custom error hierarchy.

tour.title: Authenticated Music Service Resolvers
tour.description: These three files implement the Resolver interface from Step 6 for each supported service. vkyandex.go was rewritten from a roughly 110-line anonymous-only Open Graph scraper into a dual-mode resolver: with no token it still scrapes og:title, but with Config.VKToken or Config.YMToken set it calls VK's authenticated audio.getById or Yandex's api.music.yandex.net for richer metadata. spotify.go follows the same shape -- oEmbed by default, full Web API via a cached Client Credentials token when configured -- and youtube.go shells out to yt-dlp for metadata since YouTube has no public oEmbed-equivalent for song details.
tour.languageLesson: Each resolver degrades gracefully from an authenticated path to an anonymous fallback rather than failing outright when credentials are absent -- a resilience pattern worth recognizing whenever a service integration has an optional API key.

tour.title: Audio Streaming Pipeline
tour.description: Once a Track is resolved, QMix has to actually play it. stream.go defines the StreamBackend interface and the Track/Result types that flow through it. ytdlp.go is the concrete implementation: it shells out to yt-dlp to resolve a playable URL, wrapping that expensive call in cache.go's generic TTL cache with singleflight-style deduplication so concurrent requests for the same track don't trigger redundant resolutions. proxy.go then forwards the resolved audio to the client over HTTP, validating Range headers so seeking and partial playback work correctly.
tour.languageLesson: cache.go's generic Cache[K,V] with a Do(key, loader) method is Go's singleflight pattern: concurrent callers for the same key share one in-flight computation instead of each triggering a duplicate (and here, expensive) yt-dlp invocation.

tour.title: Shared Build Info & Versioning
tour.description: Every QMix artifact -- the qmix server, the token-vk/token-ym CLIs, the Docker image, and the Android APK -- needs to agree on one version identity. buildinfo.go computes that single validated tuple (version, commit, dirty flag, Android versionCode) from Git at build time and exposes it at runtime via linker-injected variables and a --version flag, which is exactly what cmd/qmix/main.go delegated to back in Step 2. The version CLI in internal/buildinfo/cmd/version renders that same metadata as JSON, env, or -ldflags-ready text so non-Go build steps (Docker, Gradle) can consume it, and docs/versioning.md documents the whole scheme end to end, including the Android versionCode formula.
tour.languageLesson: Go's -ldflags "-X pkg.Var=value" mechanism injects string values into package variables at link time -- the standard way to stamp a binary with version/commit info without a config file, and the reason buildinfo.go's variables are set at build, not read at runtime.

tour.title: Containerization & Deployment
tour.description: The Dockerfile packages the qmix binary from Step 2 into a minimal Alpine image using a multi-stage build, passing VERSION/COMMIT/DIRTY/ANDROID_VERSION_CODE as build args sourced from the buildinfo tool in Step 9 and stamping them into both the binary (via -ldflags) and OCI image labels. It bundles yt-dlp for the streaming pipeline from Step 8 and explicitly upgrades libcrypto3/libssl3 to close a specific CVE. docker-compose.yml then runs that image as a single `backend` service, publishing port 8180->8080 with memory limits and restart policy, and optionally passing through an HTTP(S) proxy for yt-dlp.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds keep the final image small by discarding the Go toolchain and build-time dependencies after compilation -- only the compiled binary and its runtime dependencies (here, yt-dlp and updated OpenSSL libraries) make it into the final Alpine layer.

tour.title: CI/CD & Backend Test Suite
tour.description: ci.yml is the main pipeline: it enforces a repository-wide Cyrillic-free policy (this codebase was fully translated from Russian to English), lints, builds, runs unit tests behind a >=95% coverage gate, runs a mandatory HTTP integration tier, gates live-service tests behind secrets, and builds/smoke-tests the Dockerfile from Step 10 including a CVE regression check. Makefile mirrors these steps for local development, computing the same buildinfo version metadata and enforcing the same Cyrillic guard before linting. integration_mandatory_test.go is that mandatory tier in code: it boots a real HTTP server and exercises full request flows end to end -- healthz, room lifecycle, SSE delivery, resolver-mocked add-track, and audio streaming -- as a required, always-on CI gate.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows separate CI concerns into tiers with different trust levels: unit tests run unconditionally, mandatory integration tests always run and block merges, while live-service tests are secret-gated so missing credentials skip rather than fail the build.

tour.title: Architecture Docs & the Android Bridge
tour.description: ARCHITECTURE.md ties together everything from Steps 2-11 into a single reference: the Go+SSE backend stack, the Resolver/StreamBackend plugin interfaces, the in-memory data model, the REST/SSE API surface, and the docker-compose deployment topology with its CI gates. android/README.md is the equivalent entry point for the newer half of the project -- the Android TV client -- documenting its pinned toolchain (JDK 17, Gradle 8.13, Compose for TV, Media3) and noting that its APK version is derived at build time from the same buildinfo CLI covered in Step 9, directly linking the two stacks.

tour.title: Android Entry Point & App Wiring
tour.description: MainActivity.kt is the Android TV app's single Activity and entry point, mirroring the role cmd/qmix/main.go played for the backend in Step 2. It obtains a shared HostSessionController from QMixApplication -- the Application subclass that lazily constructs that controller with a configured OkHttpClient and the default backend/guest origin -- mirrors the controller's state into Compose UI state, and renders the hosting screen wired to the controller's actions.
tour.languageLesson: QMixApplication acts as a minimal hand-rolled dependency-injection container: rather than pulling in a DI framework, it lazily builds the one shared controller the Activity needs, a common lightweight pattern in smaller Android apps.

tour.title: Hosting Flow: State, Networking & Invites
tour.description: This cluster implements the TV host's room-creation experience. HostSessionController is an observable state machine -- Setup, Pending, Invitation, Error, RoomPlaceholder -- that validates backend/guest URLs and drives room creation. RoomApiClient is the OkHttp client it calls into, implementing create/get/skip against the same /rooms endpoints exposed by handlers.go back in Step 4, with strict JSON parsing and HTTP-status-to-exception mapping. GuestInvite builds the shareable invitation (room code plus guest URL, deliberately omitting the host-only token) and renders it as a QR bitmap, and HostingScreen is the Jetpack Compose UI that renders all of these states for a TV remote.
tour.languageLesson: HostSessionController models UI state as a closed set of named states (Setup/Pending/Invitation/Error) rather than a grab-bag of booleans -- Kotlin's sealed classes are the idiomatic tool for exactly this kind of exhaustive, compiler-checked state machine.

tour.title: Media3 Playback Engine & Android Build Scaffolding
tour.description: PlaybackEngine.kt defines the public playback contract -- PlaybackMedia, PlaybackState, and structured PlaybackError kinds -- that the UI layer programs against, deliberately decoupled from any specific media library. Media3PlaybackEngine.kt implements that contract by translating a lower-level PlayerBackend's events into published state snapshots, and ExoPlayerBackend.kt is the concrete Media3 ExoPlayer implementation that ultimately plays the audio streamed by the Range proxy from Step 8. build.gradle.kts closes the loop back to Step 9 by deriving the app's versionCode/versionName from the shared Go buildinfo CLI, and android.yml is the Android counterpart to Step 11's backend CI: it builds, lints, and unit-tests the app, then boots a hardware-accelerated TV emulator to run instrumentation tests behind a coverage gate.
tour.languageLesson: Separating PlaybackEngine (the contract) from Media3PlaybackEngine/ExoPlayerBackend (the Media3-specific implementation) means the UI and controller code never depend on ExoPlayer types directly -- if QMix ever swapped media libraries, only this layer would need to change.
